sections.title: PW-4: Advanced Playwright Browser Operations
sections.body:
# PW-4: Advanced Playwright Browser Operations

Playwright Masterclass · Python + TypeScript · AI Engineering · Production Automation

Until now, we have learned browser architecture, locators, element interactions, automatic waiting, assertions and synchronization.

Now we will learn how to handle complex real-world applications where users open multiple tabs, upload documents, download AI-generated reports, authenticate into applications, interact with embedded webpages and maintain browser session state.

These concepts are particularly useful when developing **agentic AI browser tools, RAG applications and enterprise automation frameworks.**

## Learning roadmap

| Concept | Interview priority |
|--------|--------|
| Multiple tabs and pages | Critical |
| Popups and browser events | Critical |
| Iframes and nested frames | Critical |
| JavaScript alerts, confirms and prompts | High |
| File uploads and file chooser events | Critical |
| File downloads | Critical |
| Screenshots and videos | High |
| Cookies and browser storage | Critical |
| Authentication state reuse | Critical |
| Persistent browser contexts | High |
| Browser permissions | High |
| Device emulation | High |
| Shadow DOM | Critical |
| Production browser security | Critical |
| RAG and AI report automation lab | Critical |

**Allocated study time:** 1 hour in our accelerated curriculum, with additional implementation practice recommended.

sections.title: Multiple tabs and pages
sections.body:
## 1.1 Storytelling: A researcher working with multiple documents

Imagine an AI researcher working in a browser.

The researcher opens four tabs:

- Tab 1: AI chatbot.
- Tab 2: LangGraph documentation.
- Tab 3: FastAPI documentation.
- Tab 4: Generated research report.

The researcher can switch between these tabs, extract information and compare results.

Playwright can control all these tabs programmatically without launching a separate browser for each one.

## 1.2 Browser architecture revision

Each browser context can contain several independently controlled pages.

A `Page` is an individual browser tab or popup window. You do not need to switch a global driver handle before interacting with another page.

You simply use the appropriate Page object.

## 1.3 Create multiple tabs

### Python

```python
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:

    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=False)

    try:

        context = browser.new_context()

        page1 = context.new_page()

        page2 = context.new_page()

        page1.goto("https://example.com")

        page2.goto("https://example.org")

        print(page1.title())

        print(page2.title())

        print(len(context.pages))

    finally:

        browser.close()
```

### TypeScript

```typescript
import { chromium } from "playwright";

const browser = await chromium.launch({
    headless: false
});

try {

    const context = await browser.newContext();

    const page1 = await context.newPage();

    const page2 = await context.newPage();

    await page1.goto("https://example.com");

    await page2.goto("https://example.org");

    console.log(await page1.title());

    console.log(await page2.title());

    console.log(context.pages().length);

} finally {

    await browser.close();
}
```

## 1.4 Selenium vs Playwright tab handling

Since Selenium traditionally uses window handles, the equivalent workflow commonly looks like this:

```python
handles = driver.window_handles

driver.switch_to.window(handles[1])

print(driver.title)
```

Playwright:

```python
print(page2.title())
```

| Selenium | Playwright |
|--------|--------|
| Window handles | Page objects |
| Switch active window | Directly interact with Page |
| `driver.window_handles` | `context.pages` |
| `driver.switch_to.window()` | Usually unnecessary |
| `driver.close()` | `page.close()` |

Playwright also supports `bring_to_front()` in Python and `bringToFront()` in TypeScript when bringing a tab to the foreground is specifically required.

## 1.5 Interactive multi-tab browser laboratory

## Browser context simulator

One browser context ·  open pages

Current visual tab

[New page] [Close page] [Reset]

Available Page objects

Playwright can interact with any open Page object, not just the visually selected tab.

sections.title: Popups and new browser tabs
sections.body: ## 2.1 Storytelling: Opening a citation from an AI chatbot Imagine asking a RAG chatbot a question. The chatbot generates an answer with three citations. You click a citation, and the original document opens in another browser tab. Your automation now needs to capture that newly opened page, verify its contents and optionally return to the original chatbot. ## 2.2 How a popup is created HTML: ```html View source document ``` JavaScript: ```javascript window.open("/documents/rag", "_blank"); ``` Both can create a new Page that Playwright can capture. ```svg ``` ## 2.3 Capture a popup from a specific page ### Python ```python with page.expect_popup() as popup_info: page.get_by_role( "link", name="View source document" ).click() popup = popup_info.value expect( popup.get_by_role("heading") ).to_have_text("RAG Documentation") print(popup.url) popup.close() ``` ### TypeScript ```typescript const popupPromise = page.waitForEvent("popup"); await page.getByRole("link", { name: "View source document" }).click(); const popup = await popupPromise; await expect( popup.getByRole("heading") ).toHaveText("RAG Documentation"); console.log(popup.url()); await popup.close(); ``` Remember the race-condition principle from PW-3: register the event waiter before triggering the popup. The popup might still be loading when you obtain its Page object. Use an appropriate assertion or navigation condition before extracting its content. ## 2.4 Page-level popup vs context-level page event Sometimes you know which page opens a popup. Sometimes you only know that a new page will be created somewhere inside the browser context. | Event | Scope | |--------|--------| | `page.on("popup")` | Popups associated with a particular page | | `context.on("page")` | New pages inside the context | | `page.waitForEvent("popup")` | Wait for a specific page's popup | | `context.waitForEvent("page")` | Wait for a new page in the context | The popup also triggers the broader context page event. Python: ```python with context.expect_page() as page_info: page.get_by_role( "link", name="Open report" ).click() report_page = page_info.value ``` TypeScript: ```typescript const newPagePromise = context.waitForEvent("page"); await page.getByRole("link", { name: "Open report" }).click(); const reportPage = await newPagePromise; ``` Prefer the more specific popup event when the triggering page is known. ## 2.5 Production AI use cases | Use case | Implementation | |--------|--------| | RAG citation validation | Open citation popup and verify document identity | | OAuth authentication | Capture and interact with an approved login popup | | AI report preview | Capture report tab and assert content | | Multi-agent research | Manage bounded independent pages | Do not simply select `context.pages()[1]` in TypeScript or `context.pages[1]` in Python and assume it is the correct popup. Other tabs may have opened unexpectedly.

sections.title: Browser events
sections.body:
## 3.1 Storytelling: A notification system

Instead of constantly asking a browser whether something happened, we can subscribe to notifications.

The browser can notify Playwright when a request starts, a response arrives, a popup opens, a file is downloaded or an uncaught JavaScript error occurs.

This is event-driven browser automation.

## 3.2 Important browser events

| Event | Meaning |
|--------|--------|
| `request` | Browser issues a network request |
| `response` | Response status and headers arrive |
| `requestfinished` | Request completes successfully at the network level |
| `requestfailed` | Request fails at the network level |
| `popup` | Page opens a popup |
| `dialog` | JavaScript dialog appears |
| `download` | File download starts |
| `filechooser` | File chooser is requested |
| `console` | Browser console message |
| `pageerror` | Uncaught page JavaScript exception |
| `close` | Page closes |
| `crash` | Page crashes |
| `frameattached` | Frame attaches |
| `framedetached` | Frame detaches |
| `framenavigated` | Frame navigates |

These events are available through the relevant Playwright objects. 

## 3.3 Persistent listener vs one-time listener

Python:

```python
def handle_console(message):

    if message.type == "error":

        print("Browser error:", message.text)

page.on("console", handle_console)

page.goto("http://localhost:8000")

page.remove_listener("console", handle_console)
```

TypeScript:

```typescript
import type { ConsoleMessage } from "playwright";

const handleConsole = (message: ConsoleMessage) => {

    if (message.type() === "error") {

        console.log("Browser error:", message.text());
    }
};

page.on("console", handleConsole);

await page.goto("http://localhost:8000");

page.off("console", handleConsole);
```

Use `once()` when a listener should handle only its next matching event.

## 3.4 Event listener vs event waiter

| Method | Purpose |
|--------|--------|
| `on()` | Observe repeated events |
| `once()` | Handle the next event |
| `off()` / `remove_listener()` | Remove a registered listener |
| `waitForEvent()` | Await a particular event in TypeScript |
| `expect_event()` | Context-managed event expectation in Python |

For a critical test operation, an awaited event expectation is often easier to synchronize than a persistent callback.

### Production warning

An HTTP 500 response does not normally trigger `requestfailed`. The browser successfully received an HTTP response, even though the server reported an error.

Use response status checks to detect HTTP failures.

Also, avoid logging raw authentication headers, sensitive console messages or unredacted request bodies in production.

sections.title: Iframes and nested frames
sections.body:
## 4.1 Storytelling: A room inside another room Imagine an enterprise dashboard that embeds an external document viewer inside the main webpage. The dashboard itself contains navigation buttons and search functionality. The embedded viewer contains its own toolbar, document controls and HTML content. Although the user sees one browser tab, there are multiple document environments. This is an iframe. ## 4.2 What is an iframe? An iframe embeds another HTML document within a webpage. ```html

AI Knowledge Base

``` The embedded document might contain: ```html

RAG Documentation

``` Ordinary page-level locators operate within the main frame unless you explicitly scope them elsewhere. ## 4.3 Page vs frame architecture ```svg ``` Each iframe introduces a separate document scope, not a separate browser tab. ## 4.4 Incorrect iframe interaction ```typescript await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Next page" }).click(); ``` If the button exists only inside the iframe, this main-frame query will not find it. ## 4.5 Correct approach: FrameLocator Python: ```python viewer = page.frame_locator( "#document-viewer" ) viewer.get_by_role( "button", name="Next page" ).click() ``` TypeScript: ```typescript const viewer = page.frameLocator( "#document-viewer" ); await viewer.getByRole("button", { name: "Next page" }).click(); ``` FrameLocator allows you to scope locators into a particular iframe. It also has strict target resolution behavior, so the iframe locator should identify the intended frame uniquely. ## 4.6 Nested frames HTML structure: ```html --> ``` Python: ```python toolbar = page.frame_locator( "#document-viewer" ).frame_locator( "#toolbar" ) toolbar.get_by_role( "button", name="Next page" ).click() ``` TypeScript: ```typescript const toolbar = page .frameLocator("#document-viewer") .frameLocator("#toolbar"); await toolbar.getByRole("button", { name: "Next page" }).click(); ``` ## 4.7 Frame vs FrameLocator Python: ```python frame = page.frame(name="document-frame") if frame is None: raise RuntimeError("Frame not found") print(frame.url) ``` TypeScript: ```typescript const frame = page.frame({ name: "document-frame" }); if (!frame) { throw new Error("Frame not found"); } console.log(frame.url()); ``` | Feature | Frame | FrameLocator | |--------|--------|--------| | Represents | Particular frame document environment | Query for entering an iframe | | Access frame URL | Yes | Not directly | | Navigation and evaluation | Supported | Primarily locator-oriented | | Dynamic iframe replacement | May need reacquisition | Can resolve the current matching iframe | | Typical UI interaction | Possible | Preferred in many cases | Inspect all current frames: ```python for frame in page.frames: print(frame.name, frame.url) ``` ```typescript for (const frame of page.frames()) { console.log(frame.name(), frame.url()); } ``` ## 4.8 Interactive iframe locator laboratory ## Choose the correct document scope **Main page** Search documents **Document viewer iframe** Zoom in **Nested toolbar iframe** Next page Target buttonCurrent selection unavailable. TypeScript locator page .getByRole("button", { name: "" }) Conceptual simulation. Select the nested toolbar to locate Next page. ## 4.9 Cross-origin iframes An iframe may load a different origin, such as an approved authentication provider or document viewer. Ordinary webpage JavaScript is restricted by the browser's same-origin policy. Playwright's frame automation APIs can nevertheless interact with supported cross-origin frames. This does not grant an AI agent permission to access every embedded application. Authorization, data handling and network restrictions still apply. ### Interview-ready answer **What is the difference between a popup and an iframe?** A popup creates a separate Page within a browser context. An iframe creates another document scope within an existing Page. I capture popups with event expectations and interact with iframe content using FrameLocator.
